keyQuotes: The I/O Processor has a very unusual architecture: although it had one physical processor, it ran 25 virtual processors with two completely different instruction sets.

The obvious approach—sending binary data unencoded—has two problems. First, in a long string of 0's or 1's, it is hard to tell how many bits were sent: 'Was that six bits or only five?' Second, such a sequence is unbalanced, so it has a 'DC component'.

mainPoints.explanation: A barrel processor cycles through virtual processors each clock cycle, guaranteeing predictable I/O bandwidth for each network port. The MSC (executive) and BCE (low-level I/O) processors have completely different instruction sets, implemented in microcode.
mainPoints.point: The IOP was a barrel processor with 25 virtual processors running two different instruction sets on one physical processor.

mainPoints.explanation: By encoding each bit with a mid-bit transition and balancing 0s and 1s, the encoding made bit separation straightforward and eliminated DC components, making it ideal for transformer-coupled, long-distance transmission.
mainPoints.point: Manchester encoding solved clock recovery and DC bias issues for the Shuttle's data buses.

mainPoints.explanation: The hybrid module integrated drivers, amplifiers, and comparators for two network ports. Transformers provided isolation and impedance matching, while TTL shift registers converted between 24-bit words and serial Manchester-encoded data.
mainPoints.point: The MIA interface board used a hybrid module and discrete components to condition analog signals.

mainPoints.explanation: Each 72-bit microinstruction step was stored by blowing fuses in PROM chips. The physical processor executed these microinstructions sequentially, switching virtual processors after each step.
mainPoints.point: The IOP's microcode was stored in fusible-link PROMs on a separate card, defining the low-level instruction sequences.

oneSentenceSummary: This article reverse-engineers two circuit boards from the Space Shuttle's I/O Processor, detailing their network interface, barrel processor architecture, Manchester encoding, and microcode-based dual-instruction-set design.
originalTitle: Examining circuit boards from the Space Shuttle's I/O Processor
summary: The author examines two physical circuit boards from the Space Shuttle's I/O Processor (IOP): a network interface board (MIA) and a PROM microcode board. The article explains the IOP's role as a multi-threaded barrel processor running 25 virtual processors with two distinct instruction sets (MSC and BCE), used to manage 24 network buses. It describes the Manchester encoding employed for robust serial data transmission, the analog circuitry in the hybrid module for signal conditioning, and the physical 'page' construction used in IBM's System/4 Pi avionics computers. The analysis includes historical context (Manchester Mark 1, Peter Kogge's work), detailed photos of the boards with annotations, and technical notes on TTL logic, shift registers, and microcode storage in fusible-link PROMs.
title: Examining circuit boards from the Space Shuttle's I/O Processor
